messages.content: What is the roots of linear equation bx + c = 0?

message.content:
For a **linear** equation  

\[
bx+c=0 \qquad (b,c\in\mathbb{R})
\]

the unknown \(x\) has only one possible value unless the coefficient of \(x\) vanishes:

| Case | Condition | Solution |
|------|-----------|----------|
| Unique root | \(b\neq 0\) | \(x=-\,\dfrac{c}{b}\) |
| No solution | \(b=0,\;c\ne 0\) | None – the line never crosses the axis |
| Infinite solutions | \(b=0,\;c=0\) | Every real number satisfies the equation |

So whenever \(b\neq 0\), the single “root” (or zero‑crossing point) is simply \(-c/b\).
message.reasoning:
The user asks "roots of linear equation bx + c = 0". That's simple: root at -c/b if b != 0; otherwise no solution or infinite solutions depending on c.
